newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua's Sandinistas woo foreign investors.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua's Sandinistas woo foreign investors.

text.p: Former President Daniel Ortega on Monday moved to ease investor fears of a Sandinista victory in Nicaragua's Oct. 20 elections, saying his government would be open to foreign investment.

"We will respect the already established rules of the game for national and foreign investment in Nicaragua and we will look for mechanisms to stimulate these investors to continue investing in our country," Ortega, the Sandinista presidential candidate, told a news conference.

His statements came after several prominent businesspeople said foreign investors would avoid Nicaragua for a few years if there is a Sandinista victory while they waited to see the new government's attitude to business.

Business leaders remembered Ortega as head of the Marxist regime that governed from 1979 to 1990, confiscating property of many foreign investors and implementing a planned economy. But this year Ortega has tried to convert the Sandinistas from fiery Marxist revolutionaries into a modern, centre-left party that respects the free market and foreign investors.
"The old policies of trade and price controls have no place in the new context facing Nicaragua and world," he said.

The strategy apparently has worked. The "new-look" Sandinistas have surged in the polls, narrowing right-wing presidential candidate Arnoldo Aleman's once seemingly insurmountable lead and making victory a possibility.
But investor doubts about the sincerity of this free-market conversion remain.

Ortega told the news conference protectionist measures should be kept in place for a time to allow weak local industries to grow in order to be able to compete with foreign companies. But he said these measures must be temporary.
"This means that one must promote protectionist measures to help national industry, but we think these measures must be temporary," he said.

Political uncertainty surrounding the election was felt last week when officials postponed the planned partial sale of Nicaragua's state-run telephone company Empresa Nicaraguense de Telecomunicaciones (Enitel) until March 31, 1997.

The head of the Enitel privatisation committee, Finance Minister Emilio Pereira, said investors had asked for the sale to be postponed until after the elections because of uncertainty surrounding the results.

But other analysts said fears of a Sandinista victory and a return of socialism were exaggerated because whatever party wins will have little economic room to manoeuvre given the agreements Nicaragua has signed with international lending institutions.
